title: Pinocchio
full_review:
The new "Pinocchio" (Miramax), live-action and shot in Italy on a lavish budget, comes nowhere near the charm of Disney's 1940 animated classic.
Academy Award-winner Roberto Benigni ("Life Is Beautiful") co-wrote the script, directed the film and stars in the title role, with wife Nicoletta Braschi co-starring as the Blue Fairy. Sadly, the film comes off as a vanity production with little of the magical quality of Carlo Collodi's 1880s Italian fairy tale translating to the big screen.

Most noticeable is the sloppy dubbing job. At the last minute Breckin Meyer was called in to voice Benigni's dialogue and the disparity between the cast's mouths and the English being spoken is frequently distracting. There really is no excuse for such a poor lip-sync when the film is the most expensive Italian production ever made.

It also requires quite a leap of faith to accept Benigni as Pinocchio. When a wooden log blows through town and lands at carpenter Geppetto's doorstep (played by Carlo Giuffre, voiced by David Suchet), he decides to carve a wooden puppet to look like the little boy he never had. Middle-aged Benigni, with his five o'clock shadow and receding hairline, doesn't exactly look the part. Benigni instantly turns manic in the part, chasing around in his clown suit and pointed hat, wanting to be a real boy but being naughty first, which always gets him in trouble.

Along the way, the Cricket (voice of John Cleese) tries to advise him and the beautiful Blue Fairy (voice of Glenn Close) rescues him, but he must learn for himself not to lie or his nose will grow. The colorful production has Pinocchio almost boiled by a soft-hearted giant, tossed in jail after his gold coins are stolen, transformed into a donkey, and reunited with his carpenter father inside the mouth of a great white shark.

All this and yet the title character is not as endearing as he should be. In fact, Benigni's broad performance assumes Pinocchio is utterly adorable when he is often bratty and tiresome. Braschi's Blue Fairy is also emotionally inert while Pinocchio's ill-fated friend Leonardo (Kim Rossi Stuart, voiced by Topher Grace) is too one-dimensional.

Children may enjoy the puppet's many misadventures and the themes of honesty, loyalty and goodness are there to be sure. But for all of Benigni's frantic running around, the story lags and the humor is minimal.
There are lovely vistas of the Tuscan countryside and an eye-pleasing production design, but "Pinocchio" should embody the wonderment of seeing life anew through a child's eyes and satisfy us when he is finally granted his wish. For that, you're better off with the animated movie.
